concepts.title: How this guide is shelved — the three-shelf rule
concepts.text:
This guide reads the alcohol × substances corpus exactly the way its research lanes built it: three shelves, one rule — every claim sits on exactly one shelf, and the shelf is named before the claim.

DOCUMENTED (this shelf): human data, official guidance, or statute text, with the source attached.

THEORETICAL (shelf 2): mechanism-reasoned and plausible, never measured in a human co-use trial.

UNSTUDIED (shelf 3): nobody has looked — no data at all, or data that never came back clean. Those keep an UNVERIFIED flag.

Why the rule matters: no controlled human trial has ever given participants alcohol together with cocaine, psilocybin, or cannabis on purpose. Every “this combination is safe” or “this combination is dangerous” sentence you meet is documented, theorized, or unstudied — and mistaking one shelf for another is how people get hurt.

⚠ Boundaries — load-bearing, not decoration: this module contains no extraction protocols, no synthesis instructions, and no dosing guidance. Solubility, solvent and history facts appear as pharmacological context only. It is public-health harm-reduction education — not medical advice, not legal advice, and never a recommendation to start, stop, or change any substance.

Scope: 98 sourced findings across six research lanes — lane 1 alcohol × cocaine (17), lane 2 alcohol × psilocybin (14), lane 3 alcohol × cannabis (22), lane 4 Michigan legal map (21), lane 5 psilocin × cocaine + alcohol (15), lane 6 microdosing × mixtures (9) — sources read 2026-10-17.

concepts.title: Lane 1 — Alcohol × cocaine: the documented record
concepts.text:
Lane 1 delivered 17 findings as a 12-line digest; every line below is the lane’s own wording with its recorded source resolved to a link.

Cocaethylene, co-use norms, and the emergency-room record:
- Mechanism: liver hCE1/hCE2 transesterifies cocaine -> cocaethylene when ethanol co-present (PMC8956485). Only known psychoactive substance formed entirely inside the body. [LANE1] Source: [PMC8956485](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8956485/)
- Human kinetics: ~17% (±6%) of IV cocaine converted under 1 g/kg ethanol; urinary benzoylecgonine -48% (PMID 14636972). [LANE1] Source: [PMID 14636972](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14636972/)
- Half-life: cocaethylene ~2h vs cocaine ~1h (reviews: 2-5x); clearance ~20% lower when both present. [LANE1]
- Psychoactive: dopamine-reuptake potency ≈ cocaine; subjects couldn't distinguish equimolar intranasal doses (double-blind). [LANE1]
- Lethality (mice): LD50 60.7 vs 93 mg/kg (PMID 1946594); >10x cardiotoxicity in reviews; dog study 2/8 cardiovascular collapse (combo) vs 0/8 (cocaine alone). [LANE1] Source: [PMID 1946594](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1946594/)
- SUDDEN DEATH: 18-25x higher with cocaethylene present (2024 systematic review PMC10935323); ~21.5x with coronary disease; co-use in ~76% of cocaine-related sudden deaths in one cohort. [LANE1] Source: [PMC10935323](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10935323/)
- ED data: SAMHSA DAWN 2024 — 392,510 cocaine ED visits, 70.2% polydrug, alcohol = top companion; combo ≈173,799 visits = #1 pairing; cocaethylene in 88% of dual-positive ED patients; cardiac arrest 6.1% (cocaethylene) vs 0.67% (cocaine alone) (PMID 36000306). [LANE1] Source: [PMID 36000306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36000306/)
- Co-use is the NORM: 74% simultaneous (CI 50-89%), 92% drink (meta-analysis PMC7450360). [LANE1] Source: [PMC7450360](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7450360/)
- Why people stack: each drug mutes the other's stop-signals (comedown softened; drunkenness blunted while BAC unchanged) (PMID 12133112, 9336321). [LANE1] Source: [PMID 12133112](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12133112/)
- Body: HR/oxygen demand super-additive; oral co-use raised cocaine Cmax 18-20%; liver ROS/LDH toxicity (PMID 8225222). [LANE1] Source: [PMID 8225222](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8225222/)
- Solvent/history (pharmacology only): cocaine HCl soluble 1:0.4 water / 1:3.2 ethanol (UNODC methods table); Brompton cocktail 1952 (90% ethanol vehicle, obsolete ~1977-79); Vin Mariani coca wine ~6 mg/fl oz (ethanol as the extracting solvent). [LANE1]
- Forensics: cocaethylene = specific simultaneous-use marker, outlives cocaine in blood (PMID 1960973); not in routine urine panels. [LANE1] Source: [PMID 1960973](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1960973/)

⚠ Lane 1 recorded boundary: pharmacology/history/forensics only; no preparation methods in public guide.

concepts.title: Lane 2 — Alcohol × psilocybin: documented chemistry and effects
concepts.text:
Findings below are the lane’s own wording, status label and recorded sources — verbatim from the payload.

Prodrug chemistry, solubility, and the only systematic human data:
- [L2] Psilocybin (O-phosphoryl-4-hydroxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine) is a phosphate-ester prodrug: it is largely converted to pharmacologically active unconjugated psilocin by alkaline phosphatases (stomach) and non-specific esterases (intestine, kidneys) BEFORE systemic absorption; psilocin then drives 5-HT2A agonist effects. — (VERIFIED) Source: Clinical Pharmacokinetics of Psilocin After Psilocybin Administration: Systematic Review and Post-Hoc Analysis ([PMC11762572](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11762572/)); Frontiers in Pharmacology 15:1391689 (2024)
- [L2] Peer-reviewed statement: 'Psilocybin is known to be soluble in water, slightly soluble in methanol and acetone, and insoluble in chloroform and hexane'; simulation study confirms the zwitterionic phosphate form is more soluble in water than in organic solvents. Hofmann-era and modern analytical chemistry uses methanol as extraction solvent. Educational implication: water-based (tea) preparations align with the molecule's chemistry; ethanol is a relatively poor solvent for psilocybin, so alcohol-based 'mushroom tinctures' are pharmacologically inefficient. Quantitative ethanol-vs-water extraction-efficiency study NOT located (see UNVERIFIED). — (VERIFIED (water/methanol); ethanol quantitative efficiency UNVERIFIED) Source: J Mol Liquids 2023, S0167732223022857 (Paul/Namba-Nzanguim et al., abstract); [PMID 17221430](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17221430/) (methanol extraction literature); Cayman Chemical psilocybin spec (caymanchem.com/product/14041)
- [L2] Mesoamerican teonanacatl use is documented as consumption of fresh or dried mushrooms, eaten with honey (Florentine Codex account quoted in an annotated bibliography of indigenous psilocybin practices) and in water-based ritual drinks; contemporary Zapotec communities in Oaxaca still use Psilocybe zapotecorum ceremonially (2025 field study). No documented traditional ethanol/tincture preparation was located - historical preparations are water/food-based. — (VERIFIED (preparations); absence-of-ethanol claim = absence of located evidence) Source: IMA Fungus 16:e148070 (2025), [PMC12125594](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12125594/); 'Indigenous psilocybin mushroom practices: An annotated bibliography' (akjournals 2054/8/1/p3); US Forest Service ethnobotany teonanacatl page
- [L2] Psilocin (not psilocybin) is the oxidation-prone species: injury or chemical/enzymatic (laccase PsiL, FeIII) oxidation converts it to blue quinoid oligomers - the 'blueing' cascade (phosphatase PsiP dephosphorylates, kinase PsiK re-phosphorylates, showing the phosphate is nature's stabilizing protecting group). Aqueous psilocin/psilocybin standard solutions are photosensitive and thermolabile; psilocin is highly unstable under all tested whole-blood storage conditions (forensic toxicology 2025); psilocybin is comparatively stable in dried mushroom biomass. CLAIM NOT SUPPORTED: ethanol as an effective psilocin preservative - no located study validates it, and the chemistry (readily oxidized phenol) argues against reliability. — (VERIFIED (degradation); ethanol-preservation claim UNVERIFIED/not supported) Source: Angew Chem 2020 ([PMC7004109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7004109/)); Chem Eur J 2021 ([PMC8457229](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8457229/)); [PMID 17002211](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17002211/) (aqueous standard stability); J Anal Toxicol 2025 (psilocin whole-blood instability); [PMID 33119971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33119971/) (biomass stability)
- [L2] Barrett et al. 2000, structured retrospective interviews with 22 experienced LSD and/or psilocybin users: among co-users, 86.7% reported COMPLETE blockade of subjective alcohol effects with LSD (remaining cases diminished); for psilocybin, 60% reported PARTIAL antagonism of subjective alcohol effects (~40% no antagonism; 1 participant reported an enhanced alcohol effect). Direction of interaction: the psychedelic attenuates the FELT effect of alcohol - a masked-intoxication risk that could promote over-drinking; the authors explicitly warn co-administration 'may pose significant health risks.' Self-report, retrospective, small n. — (VERIFIED (with stated limitations)) Source: Barrett SP, Archambault J, Engelberg MJ, Pihl RO. Hum Psychopharmacol 2000;15(7):559-565. [PMID 12404626](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12404626/)
- [L2] Documented preclinically: psilocybin-induced default-mode-network hypoconnectivity is BLUNTED in alcohol-dependent rats vs controls - chronic alcohol exposure dampens psilocybin's brain effects. In Barrett's human sample, most psilocybin co-users reported NO change in psilocybin's subjective effects when drinking, i.e., alcohol does not consistently block the psychedelic in humans; systematic human blunting data are essentially absent. — (VERIFIED in animal model; human blunting UNVERIFIED) Source: Reinwald JR et al., 'Psilocybin-induced default mode network hypoconnectivity is blunted in alcohol-dependent rats' ([PMC10721862](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10721862/)); [PMID 12404626](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12404626/)
- [L2] Psilocybin-containing mushroom exposures produce gastrointestinal clinical effects in 23% of US poison-center misuse cases (neurological 72%, cardiovascular 25%); alcohol is independently gastrically irritating and emetogenic. Amplification of nausea/vomiting when combined is biologically plausible but NOT quantified in any located co-use study; clinical psilocybin trials run alcohol-free supervised sessions, so direct trial data do not exist. — (VERIFIED separately per substance; combined amplification UNVERIFIED (mechanistic inference)) Source: Forrester MB, J Addict Dis 2020;38(4):482-488 ([PMID 32627708](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32627708/)); Bogenschutz 2022 trial design ([PMID 36001306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36001306/))
- [L2] Ethanol is diuretic and causes blackouts by blocking memory consolidation (NIAAA: 'gaps in memory... when a person drinks enough alcohol to temporarily block the transfer of memories'). Falls/injury risk during co-intoxication is supported by poison-center polysubstance encounter data (co-ingestants tracked; psilocybin encounters rose 477 to 1,441/yr 2013-2022, concentrated ages 18-44). No located study quantifies dehydration, fall, or blackout rates specifically for alcohol+psilocybin co-use - these are composite/mechanistic risks, not measured interaction outcomes. — (VERIFIED per substance; combined quantification UNVERIFIED) Source: NIAAA 'Interrupted Memories: Alcohol-Induced Blackouts' + 'Alcohol and the Brain' (niaaa.nih.gov); Montoy JCC et al., JACEP Open 2025;6(5):100231 ([PMID 40927687](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40927687/))
- [L2] 2024 National Survey Investigating Hallucinogenic Trends: 1,234 past-year psilocybin+alcohol co-users vs 1,607 alcohol-only users; co-use was associated with FEWER depressive symptoms (B=-0.57, p=.043) and, after removing cannabis/psychedelic covariates, lower anxiety symptoms. Authors: observational self-report design - NO causal inference possible; longitudinal/experimental studies needed. — (VERIFIED (with stated design limits)) Source: Hummel HM, Obrochta AN, Kerr DCR, Cservenka A. J Psychoactive Drugs (2026, published online 2026-01-30), doi:[DOI 10.1177/00220426261466154](https://doi.org/10.1177/00220426261466154)
- [L2] Supervised, alcohol-free therapy research: Bogenschutz 2022 RCT (n=95 randomized/93 analyzed; psilocybin vs diphenhydramine active placebo + 12 weeks psychotherapy): heavy-drinking days over 32 weeks = 9.7% vs 23.6% (mean difference 13.9%, 95% CI 3.0-24.7, P=.01); no serious AEs in psilocybin group. Bogenschutz 2015 proof-of-concept (n=10): abstinence increased significantly after psilocybin sessions (p<.05), gains maintained at 36 weeks, no significant treatment-related AEs. Sicignano 2024 meta-analysis: any psychedelic OR 2.16 (95% CI 1.26-3.69) for abstinence/substantial reduction, but 4 of 6 trials high risk of bias. Benvenuti 2023 (msP rats): psilocybin did NOT reduce consumption or relapse-like drinking; only a memory retrieval-reconsolidation paradigm blocked reinstatement. Framing: treatment-in-clinic science, NOT endorsement of recreational co-use. — (VERIFIED) Source: JAMA Psychiatry 2022;79(10):953-962 ([PMID 36001306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36001306/)); J Psychopharmacol 2015;29(3):289-299 ([PMID 25586396](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25586396/)); Curr Med Res Opin 2024;40(2):293-302 ([PMID 38111216](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38111216/)); Psychopharmacology 2023;240(7):1521-1530 ([PMID 37266686](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37266686/))
- [L2] HPPD = re-experiencing perceptual disturbances after hallucinogen intoxication; Type I ('flashbacks', brief/reversible; self-report estimates 5-50% of hallucinogen users) vs Type II (distressing, lasting; estimated ~4.2% - older, low-quality estimates). Evidence base is case reports and self-report surveys; risk factors incompletely characterized but anxiety vulnerability and pre-existing perceptual complaints may predict it; arousal-altering (including non-hallucinogenic) substances can worsen anxiety around symptoms. ALCOOL-specific HPPD link: NOT established in located literature. — (VERIFIED (HPPD general); alcohol association UNVERIFIED) Source: Doyle MA et al., Expert Opin Drug Saf 2022;21(6):733-743 ([PMID 35426769](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35426769/)); Halpern JH, Lerner AG, Passie T, Curr Top Behav Neurosci 2018;36:333-360 ([PMID 27822679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27822679/))
- [L2] MAPS/Zendo Project: Four Principles of Psychedelic Care (1 Create a safe space, 2 Sitting not guiding, 3 Talk through not down, 4 Difficult is not necessarily bad) - principle-based care for difficult experiences in non-ordinary states. Fireside Project: free confidential Psychedelic Support Line, call/text 62-FIRESIDE (623-473-7433), daily 11am-11pm PT; peer-support helpline study (n=884 callers): 65.9% de-escalated from distress, 29.3% said they may otherwise have been harmed, 12.5% may have called 911, 10.8% may have gone to the ER. ALCOHOL-SPECIFIC guidance was NOT found in the Zendo/MAPS/Fireside public pages checked - their frameworks apply to alcohol-involved difficult experiences (safe space, sitter, real-time support) but no published alcohol-specific session guidance exists in these sources; clinical trials, by contrast, conduct sessions in supervised, substance-controlled settings. — (VERIFIED (orgs/principles/outcomes); alcohol-specific org guidance = none located) Source: maps.org Zendo Project page; zendoproject.org 4 Principles PDF (2025); firesideproject.org (+FAQ); Pleet MM et al., Psychedelic Medicine 2023 ([PMC10286261](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10286261/)); Bogenschutz 2022 trial design ([PMID 36001306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36001306/))

Lane 2 recorded these safety takeaways:
- LEGAL: psilocybin is Schedule I federally and ILLEGAL in Michigan; city-level decriminalization is a separate lane-4 topic. This guide is an educational pharmacology/safety/legal aggregate - it contains NO extraction protocols, NO grow/prep instructions, and NO dosing promotion.
- Masked intoxication is the documented co-use hazard: the best human data show psychedelics (especially LSD, less consistently psilocybin) attenuate the FELT effect of alcohol, so a drinker may not sense how intoxicated they are - the Barrett authors warn the practice 'may pose significant health risks.'
- Alcohol around sessions works against the set-and-setting that psychedelic care frameworks are built on (Zendo: safe space; trials: supervised, substance-controlled sessions); impaired judgment during an altered state compounds accident/fall risk.
- Nausea/dehydration burden is additive per substance (poison-center GI effects for mushrooms; ethanol diuresis/irritation) - combined amplification is unmeasured, so treat it as a risk assumption, not a fact.
- Alcohol blackouts are established for alcohol alone (NIAAA); memory gaps during co-intoxicated altered states are plausible but unmeasured - treat as risk, not documented interaction.
- Psilocin is chemically fragile (oxidizes readily, unstable even in whole blood); folk claims that alcohol 'preserves' preparations or efficiently extracts psilocybin lack located support - water is the solvent the molecule's chemistry actually supports, and ethanol extraction is pharmacologically inefficient.
- HPPD exists (Type II est. ~4.2% of hallucinogen users in older, low-quality estimates) and anxiety-vulnerable people appear more susceptible; an alcohol link is NOT established.
- If someone struggles during or after an experience (alcohol involved or not): Zendo/MAPS peer-support principles, Fireside Support Line 62-FIRESIDE (623-473-7433, 11am-11pm PT); medical emergency = 911. Clinical psilocybin treatment for AUD is a supervised medical protocol (JAMA Psychiatry 2022), not a DIY co-use rationale.

concepts.title: Lane 3 — Alcohol × cannabis: documented co-use and Michigan product rules
concepts.text:
Findings below are the lane’s own wording, status label and recorded sources — verbatim from the payload.

Tincture history, blood THC, blackouts, driving, and Michigan statutes:
- [L3] Cannabis tinctures were mainstream US medicine: cannabis was admitted to the US Pharmacopeia as Extractum Cannabis in 1850 (3rd ed.; one authoritative account dates it 1851) and stayed official through the 11th revision; USP revisions described how to prepare ethanol extracts and tinctures of dried flowers; cannabis was dropped from the 12th edition in 1942, five years after the 1937 Marihuana Tax Act made prescription impractical — removal was administrative, not pharmacological. — (verified (multiple independent sources; minor 1850-vs-1851 date discrepancy noted)) Source: National Academies 2017, Health Effects of Cannabis and Cannabinoids (NAP 24625), ch.2; historyofcannabis.org USP pharmacopoeia page
- [L3] Ethanol is the classic cannabis solvent: USP-era pharmacists standardized maceration/percolation of cannabis flower in alcohol; cannabinoids are highly lipophilic (logP ~6-7), which is why high-proof alcohol extracts them efficiently. High-proof ethanol extracts both acidic cannabinoids (THCA) and neutral THC. — (verified (history + chemistry)) Source: NAP 24625 ch.2 (USP tincture/extract monographs); [PMC5549534](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5549534/) (cannabinoid chemistry)
- [L3] Chemistry caveat for tinctures: the plant stores THC mainly as THCA, the non-intoxicating acidic precursor; decarboxylation to psychoactive delta-9-THC requires heat (smoking/vaping/baking) or processing steps. Alcohol extraction alone does not fully decarboxylate, which is why commercial tincture producers decarb and why 'total THC' is the regulated metric. — (verified (peer-reviewed reviews)) Source: [PMC5549534](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5549534/) (THCA non-psychoactive, decarboxylates with heat); [PMC9225410](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9225410/) (acidic cannabinoid decarboxylation review); [PMC12300620](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12300620/) (GMP extract oil requires decarb step)
- [L3] Michigan law explicitly recognizes tinctures: MCL 333.27953(m) defines 'marihuana-infused product' as 'a topical formulation, tincture, beverage, edible substance, or similar product containing marihuana and other ingredients and that is intended for human consumption.' Alcohol tinctures are therefore a recognized preparation category in MI's regulated market. — (verified (statute text)) Source: [MCL 333.2795](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-333.2795)3(m)
- [L3] MI consumer-safety rules exist for dosing: under R 420.404 and the CRA technical bulletin (Apr 24, 2025), infused products are lab-tested with total THC/CBD printed on labels, delta-8 capped at 10% of total THC, per-serving/per-container THC caps apply (bulletin example: 200 mg max per adult-use gummy container; secondary sources consistently report 10 mg/serving adult-use edibles and 100 mg max per beverage container), and — directly relevant to tinctures — CRA guidance says tinctures and oil-based drops should use containers that enforce serving-size limits via calibrated droppers or calibrated oral syringes. — (mostly verified (calibrated-dropper requirement + delta-8 cap + 200 mg gummy example from primary bulletin; exact table values corroborated by secondary reproductions — flagged)) Source: CRA Technical Bulletin 'Maximum THC Concentrations for Marijuana-Infused Products' (Apr 24, 2025, R 420.404); CRA Allowable Potency Variance bulletin (10% variance table); michigan.gov R 420.401-405 rule PDF
- [L3] Onset differs by route — the core overconsumption trap: inhaled cannabis hits within minutes (peak ~20-30 min, taper 2-3 h); swallowed tincture/edible onset 30-90 min (CDC: up to 2 h), peak ~2-4 h (JAMA 2024: effects can last up to ~24 h); 'sublingual' tincture is intermediate and deceptive — PK studies of the ethanol-based oromucosal spray (nabiximols) show Tmax ~1 h and an 11-hydroxy-THC/THC ratio similar to oral dosing, i.e., a substantial fraction of any tincture dose is swallowed and behaves like an edible. — (verified (CDC, JAMA, controlled PK study); sublingual-fraction generalization to consumer tinctures is well-grounded extrapolation) Source: CDC Cannabis and Poisoning; JAMA Intern Med 2024 (edibles explainer); [PMC5260817](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5260817/) (Tasty THC: edibles PK); [PMID 23179176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23179176/) (THC/CBD oromucosal spray phase I PK)
- [L3] Alcohol before cannabis raises THC exposure: in a controlled human trial (NIDA-funded), ethanol (0.35/0.7 g/kg) before smoking significantly increased plasma THC, sped detection of marijuana effects, and produced more euphoria episodes vs placebo ethanol — likely via vasodilation/increased absorption (Lukas & Orozco 2001). The reverse also holds: cannabis smoking slows ethanol absorption and dulls perceived alcohol effects, which can lead people to drink more. — (verified in controlled lab studies; caveat: small samples, male volunteers) Source: [PMID 11543984](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11543984/) (Lukas & Orozco 2001, Drug Alcohol Depend); [PMC7064425](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7064425/) (discussion citing Lukas 1992 reverse direction)
- [L3] Replication with modern vaporized cannabis: NIDA's Huestis lab (2015, Clinical Chemistry) — low-dose alcohol (~0.065% peak BrAC) 10 min before vaporized cannabis significantly raised median peak blood THC and 11-OH-THC vs no alcohol (high-THC session: 67.5 vs 42.2 ug/L THC), possibly via increased cardiac output/pulmonary capillary flow or less careful self-titration while intoxicated. — (verified (controlled crossover study, N=19 completers); effect substantial mainly at the high-THC dose — the low-dose difference was small) Source: [PMC4749481](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4749481/) (Hartman et al. 2015); AACC/ScienceDaily release May 27, 2015
- [L3] Driving impairment is at least additive and practically dangerous: cannabis roughly doubles crash-involvement risk (Hartman & Huestis 2013 review); combining cannabis with alcohol enhances impairment, especially lane weaving (SDLP). Simulator study (N=18): cannabis+alcohol SDLP effects were additive rather than synergistic; blood THC 8.2 ug/L during driving produced SDLP impairment like 0.05% BrAC, 13.1 ug/L like 0.08% BrAC. An on-road study cited by Huestis: low-dose THC (100/200 ug/kg) combined with 0.04% BAC produced impairment resembling 0.09% BAC — near Michigan's 0.08 threshold. — (verified (experimental + epidemiologic)) Source: Hartman & Huestis 2013, Clin Chem 59:478-492 ([PMID 23220273](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23220273/)); Hartman et al. 2015 SDLP simulator paper; AACC Clinical Chemistry podcast transcript (Huestis)
- [L3] 'Cross-fading' is real and measurable: an ecological-momentary-assessment study (2025) found co-use produced greater momentary subjective intoxication than cannabis-only (strongest within 0-90 min of each other) and more stimulation AND more 'bad effects' than cannabis-only when co-used within 0-30 min. Laboratory reviews consistently find co-administration impairs behavioral/neurocognitive measures more than either substance alone. — (verified) Source: [PMID 39970575](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39970575/) (Bedillion & Ansell 2025); [PMC8855954](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8855954/) (co-use mechanisms review); [PMC7363401](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7363401/) (Yurasek 2017 co-use review: additive impairment)
- [L3] Blackouts are the signature simultaneous-use harm: among college students who used both substances, the ONLY consequence class that still differed between simultaneous (SAM) and concurrent-but-not-simultaneous (CAM) users after full covariate adjustment was blackouts. Prevalence: ~56% of SAM users reported blackouts vs ~37% CAM and ~28% alcohol-only. Alcohol-induced blackouts also amplify the link between cannabis quantity and cannabis-related consequences. — (verified (large survey studies)) Source: [PMC7064425](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7064425/) (Jackson et al. 2020); NIDA Notes June 2021 summary; [PMC11178058](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11178058/) (blackout moderation study)
- [L3] Emergency-department signal: SAMHSA DAWN (Jan 2021-Sep 2023) counted ~8.57M alcohol-related ED visits — the most of any substance, double opioids or cannabis; ~1 in 5 alcohol-related visits were polysubstance, and among those, 1 in 3 involved cannabis (for under-21 visits: 31% polysubstance, and 2 in 3 of those involved cannabis). A 2024 DAWN report shows alcohol+drug visits at 7.6% of all substance-related ED visits. — (verified (federal surveillance data)) Source: SAMHSA DAWN rpt44498 (alcohol report); SAMHSA DAWN rpt56259 (2024 polysubstance report)
- [L3] Cannabis' antiemetic effect can mask alcohol poisoning: combining the two may suppress vomiting, one of the body's warning signals for dangerous alcohol levels — meaning a cross-faded person can progress further into alcohol toxicity without the usual cue. This is documented in the peer-reviewed co-use literature. — (verified (mechanistic, cited in Jackson 2020; underlying lab study Sodergalm/Soderpalm 2001)) Source: [PMC7064425](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7064425/) (discussing antiemetic masking); Yurasek 2017 review
- [L3] Co-use drives more drinking: NIDA Notes summaries of diary studies report young adults drank more alcohol on days they also used marijuana than on alcohol-only days, and co-users report more harms on co-use days. Heavy-drinking occasions (5+/4+ drinks) combined with cannabis show the most pronounced consequence escalation. — (verified (EMA/diary studies)) Source: NIDA Notes (June 2021); [PMC7363401](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7363401/); [PMC9059839](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9059839/) (SAM scoping review)
- [L3] Anxiety/paranoia interactions: acute THC overconsumption commonly produces anxiety, panic, paranoia, tachycardia, nausea and dizziness — cannabis-induced tachycardia was the most-cited cardiac finding in a systematic review (highlighted in 61% of reviewed studies). Co-use moments carry higher 'bad effects' ratings than cannabis-only moments, and CDC warns combining cannabis with alcohol increases harm risk including unknown drug-drug interactions. People with cardiac conditions face added risk (arrhythmia reports). — (verified for symptoms and co-use 'bad effects'; attributing specific anxiety amplification to the interaction per se is limited) Source: [PMID 32267189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32267189/) (cannabis dysrhythmia systematic review); [PMID 39970575](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39970575/) (bad effects EMA); CDC alcohol+other drugs page; CDC Cannabis FAQ
- [L3] 'Greening out' is an informal community term, not a formal clinical diagnosis — UNVERIFIED as a clinical entity. What IS documented: the acute overconsumption cluster it describes (nausea/vomiting, dizziness, sweating, anxiety/panic, tachycardia) and poison-control guidance that symptoms typically pass within hours while hydration/rest/safe setting help; and that alcohol co-use and delayed-onset edibles/beverages increase overconsumption risk. — (partially verified — symptom cluster documented; the term itself lacks a peer-reviewed case definition) Source: CDC Cannabis FAQ (overconsumption); [PMID 32267189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32267189/); NIDA/poison-control-style guidance via CDC poisoning page
- [L3] Evidence-quality check on 'alcohol increases THC absorption/effects': SUPPORTED — two independent controlled human studies (Lukas 2001 smoking; Hartman/Huestis 2015 vaporizing) + 2025 EMA subjective data all point the same direction. LIMITS: small Ns, mostly male occasional users, and the blood-level jump was substantial mainly at high THC doses (35.3 vs 32.7 ug/L at low dose; 67.5 vs 42.2 at high dose). The better-established practical fact is impairment ADDITIVITY, not absorption magnitude. — (supported with explicit caveats) Source: [PMID 11543984](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11543984/); [PMC4749481](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4749481/); [PMID 39970575](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39970575/)
- [L3] Next-day effects split cleanly by substance: ALCOHOL hangover is well documented; a 2023 systematic review of THC 'next day' effects (20 studies, 458 participants, 345 performance tests >8 h post-THC) found little high-quality evidence of next-day impairment from cannabis alone (16/20 studies: no effect; the 5 positive studies were all >18 years old with methodological limits). But the 'window of impairment' meta-regression shows 3-10 h of impairment after use — LONGER for oral THC than inhaled — so morning-after driving after a tincture night is still not cleared. Direct evidence that combining compounds hangover severity: UNVERIFIED (inferred from separate literatures). — (verified for the review findings; compounding claim flagged) Source: [PMC9940812](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9940812/) (McCartney et al. 2023, Cannabis Cannabinoid Res)
- [L3] MI baseline legality: recreational cannabis is legal for adults 21+ under the Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (approved by voters Nov 6, 2018; MCL 333.27951 et seq.). Lawful: possess/transport up to 2.5 oz in public (max 15 g concentrate), 10 oz + 12 plants at home, give up to 2.5 oz to another adult (MCL 333.27955). Not authorized: consuming in public (except municipality-authorized designated consumption areas under 21-exclusion, MCL 333.27954(1)(e)); MI CRA rules define licensed 'designated consumption establishments' (R 420.1). — (verified (statute text)) Source: [MCL 333.2795](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-333.2795)4; [MCL 333.2795](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-333.2795)5; R 420.1 definitions
- [L3] The direct answer to 'can MI dispensaries sell cannabis drinks WITH alcohol?': NO — Michigan's Liquor Control Code (MCL 436.1914b, added by HB 4668, 2019) prohibits any person from using, offering for use, possessing, selling, or offering for sale marihuana-infused beer, wine, mixed wine drink, mixed spirit drink, or spirits — defined as those beverages containing 'any amount of marihuana.' Violation is a misdemeanor (penalty per Sec. 914b/909), with an exception only for bona fide research institutions. So THC beverages exist in MI's dispensary market, but they are alcohol-free by law; alcohol licensees also cannot add cannabis. — (verified (statute text retrieved verbatim)) Source: [MCL 436.1914b](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-436.1914b); Michigan House Bill 4668 legislative analysis (2017-2018 session, enacted 2019)
- [L3] MI transport/open-container analog: usable marihuana in or on a motor vehicle must be enclosed in a case carried in the trunk (or, no trunk, not readily accessible from the interior) — MCL 750.474, misdemeanor up to 93 days/$500; medical marihuana-infused products must be in a sealed, labeled package in the trunk (MCL 333.26424b, civil fine up to $250); consuming or smoking in the passenger area on a public way is expressly not authorized by MRTMA (MCL 333.27954(1)(g)). Separately, driving with ANY amount of a Schedule 1 substance (marihuana/THC) in the body is a crime regardless of measured impairment — MCL 257.625(8), zero-tolerance; MRTMA does not preempt it (People v Perry, 338 Mich App 363 (2021)); only registered medical patients hold the Koon exception. — (verified (statutes + case law)) Source: [MCL 750.474](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-750.474); [MCL 333.2642](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-333.2642)4b; [MCL 333.2795](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-333.2795)4(1)(g); [MCL 257.625(8)](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-257.625(8)) + Michigan Courts benchbook; People v Koon 494 Mich 1 (2013); People v Perry (2021)
- [L3] Credible harm-reduction guidance for people who do combine: CDC — do not drink alcohol when using other drugs including cannabis; never drive (designated driver/rideshare). Canada's Lower-Risk Cannabis Use Guidelines — wait at least 6 h after cannabis before driving; combining alcohol+cannabis should categorically be avoided because impairment effects multiply. Washington State LCB — avoid mixing; buy tested, licensed product; keep original packaging so dose is known. For tincture/edible users: CDC/JAMA/Colorado — start low (2.5-5 mg, well under MI's 10 mg max serving), wait ≥90 min-4 h before redosing, never redose on delay, food slows absorption, stable seated setting, hydrate, treats blackouts as a stop signal, be aware cannabis may mask alcohol-poisoning vomiting cues. — (verified (official public-health guidance)) Source: CDC alcohol+other drugs; CDC cannabis driving; CDC poisoning page; Health Canada LRCUG (canada.ca + CAMH PDF); WA State LCB; Colorado cannabis.gov edibles safety; JAMA Intern Med 2024

Lane 3 recorded these safety takeaways:
- Do not drive or operate machinery for at least 6 hours after cannabis (LRCUG) — and longer after swallowed tinctures/edibles (impairment window 3-10 h, longer for oral routes); in Michigan, ANY detectable THC in the body while operating a vehicle is a zero-tolerance crime (MCL 257.625(8)), independent of how you feel.
- Start low, go slow, and wait out the onset: tincture swallowed = treat as an edible (30 min-2 h onset, 2-4 h peak); never redose because 'nothing happened yet.' Use the label's mg-per-serving and the calibrated dropper the CRA requires.
- If combining: keep alcohol to one standard drink per hour at most, dose cannabis first and slowly, and expect the alcohol to amplify the high (higher blood THC) — the cross-fade is a dose-stacking risk, not a party trick.
- Know the masked-warning problem: cannabis' antiemetic effect can hide alcohol poisoning; if someone cross-faded becomes quiet, sleepy, hard to rouse, or cold/clammy — check on them actively and call for help when in doubt.
- Sit-down preparation: consume seated in a familiar, safe setting with food beforehand and water on hand; avoid combining at all with cardiac conditions (cannabis tachycardia/arrhythmia reports) or anxiety histories.
- Transport legally in MI: cannabis in a case in the trunk or out of reach, never consumed in the passenger area; public use only in municipality-authorized designated consumption areas.
- Treat blackouts as a stop signal — simultaneous use is what most strongly predicts blackouts, and blackout history amplifies cannabis-related consequences.
- Don't buy the combo product anywhere: in Michigan, marihuana-infused alcoholic beverages are illegal to sell, possess, or use (misdemeanor) — any 'cannabis drink' at a bar with alcohol in it is either illegal or mislabeled.

concepts.title: Lane 5 — Psilocin × cocaine and alcohol: the documented record
concepts.text:
Findings below carry the lane’s status label and — where the lane recorded one — its safety takeaway, verbatim from the payload.

Psilocin as the active molecule — human PK, case literature, published guidance:
- [L5] Psilocybin is a prodrug: alkaline phosphatase (plus nonspecific esterases) dephosphorylates it to psilocin in the gut/liver, essentially completely before systemic absorption; psilocin is the actual effector that crosses the blood-brain barrier and acts as a partial agonist at 5-HT2A/2C and 5-HT1A receptors. — So what: Education should target psilocin as the active molecule — every co-use interaction acts on psilocin's levels or effects, not the phosphate ester. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13715851/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13715851/); [https://doi.org/[DOI 10.1080/03602532.2016.1278228](https://doi.org/10.1080/03602532.2016.1278228](https://doi.org/10.1080/03602532.2016.1278228](https://doi.org/10.1080/03602532.2016.1278228)); [https://link.springer.com/article/[DOI 10.1007/s40262-024-01454-4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40262-024-01454-4](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40262-024-01454-4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40262-024-01454-4))
- [L5] Human PK: unconjugated psilocin peaks ~2 h after oral psilocybin (Tmax range 1.05-3.71 h), terminal half-life 1.23-4.72 h, bioavailability ~52-55%; only 1.5-3.4% is excreted unchanged; main clearance is glucuronidation (UGT1A9 liver, UGT1A10 gut) and MAO/aldehyde-dehydrogenase oxidation to 4-HIAA. — So what: Because psilocin is short-lived, stimulant or alcohol exposure overlapping roughly the first 6-8 h is the window where pharmacologic stacking occurs. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://link.springer.com/article/[DOI 10.1007/s40262-024-01454-4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40262-024-01454-4](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40262-024-01454-4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40262-024-01454-4)); [https://ascpt.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/[DOI 10.1002/cpt.2821](https://ascpt.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cpt.2821](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.2821](https://ascpt.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cpt.2821))
- [L5] Cocaine binds and blocks monoamine reuptake transporters (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, serotonin) with roughly equal affinity; its sympathomimetic toxidrome is tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, agitation, with chronic risk of MI, arrhythmia, and stroke; it is vasoconstrictive and impairs heat loss. — So what: Cocaine's combined adrenergic + serotonergic (SERT) load is the mechanistic basis for concern when stacked with a 5-HT2A agonist. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430769](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430769); [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430757](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430757)
- [L5] First published case of its kind: a 42-year-old on tranylcypromine (MAOI) plus extended-release dextroamphetamine-amphetamine developed a hypertensive emergency (BP 230s/100s, chest pain, ST-elevation ECG) ~30 min after Psilocybe cubensis; catheterization was normal and he recovered; authors suspect phenylethylamine in P. cubensis + MAOI + norepinephrine releaser and explicitly warn about stimulants co-prescribed with mushroom use. — So what: Strongest published cardiovascular warning for stimulant-class co-use with psilocybin mushrooms — same sympathomimetic family as cocaine. — (VERIFIED (peer-reviewed case report; prescribed amphetamine, not cocaine)) Source: [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38903003/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38903003/); [https://bhnet.org/21273/hypertensive-crisis-linked-to-psilocybin-use-with-other-substances](https://bhnet.org/21273/hypertensive-crisis-linked-to-psilocybin-use-with-other-substances)
- [L5] TripSit rates psilocybin x cocaine 'Caution' (not 'Unsafe'): stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops leading to negative experiences; PsychonautWiki lists cocaine and amphetamines among the flagged interactions on its psilocybin mushrooms page; a community survey (N=581) recorded explicit 'do not mix with stimulants' (5.3%) and cocaine (1.4%) advice; NSDUH 2024 analysis shows psilocybin users disproportionately co-use alcohol and cocaine. — So what: Consensus HR framing for stimulant co-use: panic/anxiety amplification plus unnecessary cardiac strain — not demonstrated lethal toxicity. — (VERIFIED (as published guidance; ratings are expert-consensus, not clinical-trial data)) Source: [https://tripsit.me/factsheets/Mushrooms](https://tripsit.me/factsheets/Mushrooms); [https://psychonautwiki.org/wiki/Psilocybin_mushrooms](https://psychonautwiki.org/wiki/Psilocybin_mushrooms); [https://doi.org/[DOI 10.1186/s12954-025-01337-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12954-025-01337-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12954-025-01337-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12954-025-01337-2)); [https://news.illinois.edu/study-millions-in-the-us-report-past-year-psilocybin-use](https://news.illinois.edu/study-millions-in-the-us-report-past-year-psilocybin-use)
- [L5] Serious psilocybin-mushroom presentations cluster with polysubstance context rather than psilocin toxicity alone: documented case of magic mushrooms + alcohol + LSD co-ingestion causing AKI requiring dialysis with myocarditis in a patient with prior cocaine exposure (authors note vasoconstrictive/prothrombotic synergy); US poison-center psilocybin encounters rose 477 (2013) to 1,441 (2022); in the Global Drug Survey 2017 only 0.2% of past-year mushroom users sought emergency treatment, with mixing substances and poor mindset/setting the most reported reasons. — So what: Co-use is the risk multiplier: polysubstance context, not psilocin alone, drives most serious medical outcomes. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/[PMC12701083](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12701083/)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/[PMC12701083](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12701083/)); [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/[PMC12414881](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12414881/)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/[PMC12414881](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12414881/)); [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/[PMC9353971](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9353971/)/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/[PMC9353971](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9353971/)/)
- [L5] Peer-support and clinical HR bodies converge on 'avoid stacking': community-crowdsourced best-practices study (N=581) lists alcohol (20.8%), stimulants (5.3%), and cocaine (1.4%) among things not to mix; TripSit's chart rates psilocybin x cocaine Caution, x tramadol Unsafe, x lithium Dangerous; Drug Science (UK) states psilocybin should not be combined with other illicit drugs, alcohol, or nicotine; Johns Hopkins' guide advises sober sitters, familiar settings, and preparation for nausea/tachycardia. — So what: Teach the shared core: sober trusted company, no stimulant/alcohol stacking, plan for emergencies — these appear across every credible HR source. — (VERIFIED (as published guidance)) Source: [https://doi.org/[DOI 10.1186/s12954-025-01337-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12954-025-01337-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12954-025-01337-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12954-025-01337-2)); [https://tripsit.me/factsheets/Mushrooms](https://tripsit.me/factsheets/Mushrooms); [https://www.drugscience.org.uk/drugs/psilocybin](https://www.drugscience.org.uk/drugs/psilocybin); [https://www.hopkinsguides.com/hopkins/view/Johns_Hopkins_Psychiatry_Guide/787494/all/Harm_Reduction_and_Safety_in_Recreational_Psychedelic_Use%C2%A0](https://www.hopkinsguides.com/hopkins/view/Johns_Hopkins_Psychiatry_Guide/787494/all/Harm_Reduction_and_Safety_in_Recreational_Psychedelic_Use%C2%A0)
- [L5] Psilocybin and psilocin are controlled substances in many countries (the 2017 toxicological review's framing), while psilocybin remains an FDA-investigational, non-approved psychiatric drug (COMP360 NDA targeted for Q4 2026); cocaine retains a single FDA-approved medical use (adult nasal mucosa anesthesia) with no approved pediatric indication. Jurisdiction-level detail (Oregon services, local decriminalization) varies and should be checked locally. — So what: Community education must note that legality varies by jurisdiction and does not change the pharmacology-based safety content. — (VERIFIED at the aggregate level; jurisdiction specifics NOT enumerated here) Source: [https://doi.org/[DOI 10.1080/03602532.2016.1278228](https://doi.org/10.1080/03602532.2016.1278228](https://doi.org/10.1080/03602532.2016.1278228](https://doi.org/10.1080/03602532.2016.1278228)); [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430769](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430769); [https://www.bakerdonelson.com/fda-finalizes-guidance-on-psychedelic-drugs-for-clinical-investigations-key-implications-for-hospitals-and-trial-sponsors](https://www.bakerdonelson.com/fda-finalizes-guidance-on-psychedelic-drugs-for-clinical-investigations-key-implications-for-hospitals-and-trial-sponsors)

concepts.title: Lane 6 — Microdosing × mixtures: the documented evidence base
concepts.text:
Findings below carry the lane’s status label and — where the lane recorded one — its safety takeaway, verbatim from the payload.

What the trials, surveys and screening frameworks actually show:
- [L6] Microdosing is defined in the literature as ingestion of sub-perceptual/sub-hallucinogenic doses (~1/10 to 1/20 of a standard psychoactive dose) of classic psychedelics, most commonly LSD and psilocybin, typically 2-4x/week for weeks to months. Documented protocol names: Fadiman-style one-day-on/two-days-off (every-3rd-day); survey data (Anderson 2020, n=909) show median self-reported doses of 13 mcg LSD and 0.3 g dried mushrooms, with the 1-day-on/2-days-off schedule most common (35.9%). Some users also microdose MDMA and cannabis. — So what: For educators: describing published protocol ranges is educational fact; dose accuracy is a documented problem - Global Drug Survey 2017 found 64.3% of LSD microdosers dosed by 'guess work' from illegally sourced tabs, meaning many users are not actually getting sub-perceptual doses. — (high) Source: Anderson et al. 2020, J Psychopharmacol ([PMID 32108529](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32108529/)); Fadiman 2011 as documented in literature; Rouaud/Calder/Hasler 2024, J Psychopharmacol ([PMID 38214279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38214279/)); US adult prevalence survey [PMC13155376](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13155376/)
- [L6] The evidence problem: controlled studies largely fail to replicate survey self-report benefits. The self-blinding citizen-science trial (Szigeti 2021, n=191, largest placebo-controlled psychedelic trial) found improvements in both microdose and placebo arms with no significant between-group differences; participant GUESS drove outcomes (21 of 22 comparisons favored the microdose guess regardless of capsule contents). The Translational Psychiatry double-blind trial (2022, n=34) found subjective effects only in participants who broke blind, no creativity/cognition/wellbeing benefits, and small impairments on some tasks. Kaertner 2021 found baseline expectancy predicted improvement but explained only 5-8% of variance. However, a 2024 rapid review (PMC11311906, 19 controlled studies) argues 'microdosing is a placebo' is premature: small samples, possible insufficient doses, dose-dependent effects observed, expectancy measured impact small. — So what: Teach the community: self-reported benefits are heavily confounded by expectancy; anyone teaching microdosing as evidence-based therapy is overstating the science. — (high) Source: Szigeti et al. 2021, eLife/[PMC7925122](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7925122/); van Elk/Transl Psychiatry 2022 (nature.com/articles/s41398-022-02039-0); Kaertner et al. 2021, Sci Rep; Szigeti/Nutt/Erritzoe 2023 'active placebo' reanalysis ([DOI 10.1038/s41598-023-34938-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-34938-7)); Polito & Liknaitzky 2024 rapid review [PMC11311906](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11311906/)
- [L6] Psychological risk flags: (a) psychosis-spectrum - personal history of psychotic disorder or first-degree family history is a near-universal exclusion in psilocybin trials (Johns Hopkins 2008 framework: excludes personal/1st-2nd degree family psychosis, bipolar I/II, lithium, MAOIs); a 2025 argument for nuance exists re: bipolar family history (PMC11658676), but the conservative consensus contraindication stands; (b) dependency-on-ritual: classic psychedelics show low abuse/dependence liability (weak reinforcement preclinically, tolerance develops, no documented withdrawal) but survey work documents ritual-anchored use patterns, and the practice of daily-dosing regimens contradicts tolerance data; mushroom content variability also creates documented accidental-dose risk (Johnson/Garcia-Romeu CSA review). — So what: Screen questions educators can teach: any personal/family psychosis or bipolar history? currently on lithium or MAOIs? is the schedule driven by need rather than protocol? Those three catch most documented risk patterns. — (high) Source: [PMC11658676](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11658676/) (Bipolar family history nuance); [PMC6791528](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6791528/) (8-factor abuse liability review); Johns Hopkins 2008 safety framework as cited in literature; nature.com/articles/s41380-025-03240-5 (NHP review)
- [L6] Safe-consumption education consensus (community + harm-reduction literature): the documented beginner-safety core is - never assume dose (mushroom potency varies widely; LSD tabs mislabeled), do not mix other substances (alcohol, stimulants, cannabis, MDMA) in the dosing window, screen for cardiac and psychiatric risk factors, do not dose alone at first (experienced sitter), plan set/setting and no driving, journal doses and effects for honest self-observation (helps separate expectancy from effect given finding #2), use peer support/helplines (Fireside-style phone peer support documented to de-escalate distress and reduce EMS burden), and integrate afterward. Sources note most lay advice is community-generated and sometimes contradictory - empirical support is thin for many specific rules. — So what: Frame everything as risk reduction, not safety guarantee - the literature itself stresses these practices are consensus-based, not trial-proven. — (moderate) Source: [PMC12495836](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12495836/) harm reduction scoping review; [PMC12648905](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12648905/) best-practices survey; Johnson et al. safety framework; Lea et al. 2020 harm reduction practices
- [L6] Michigan legal reality (one line for educators): psilocybin remains Schedule 1 under Michigan state law (MCL 333.7404) and federal law; Ann Arbor (2020), Washtenaw County (2021), Detroit (2021), Hazel Park (2022), Ferndale (2023), and Ypsilanti (2024) have only DEPRIORITIZED enforcement - deprioritization is not legality, and state/federal enforcement power is unchanged. Deep legal map belongs to lane 4. — So what: Educators should present decrim cities accurately: lowest enforcement priority != legal to sell, possess, or distribute. — (high) Source: Ann Arbor Resolution R-20-362 (Sept 21, 2020); Detroit Proposal E (Nov 2021); psilocybinlegalization.com/record/michigan

concepts.title: Lane 4 — Michigan legal map: the statutes as written
concepts.text:
Michigan law as the lane read it from primary sources, with the two citation corrections the original brief needed (cocaine = MCL 333.7214(a)(iv) Schedule 2; psilocybin = MCL 333.7212(1)(c)).

One statute, corrected citations, the decrim map, and second chances:
- [L4] 'Operating while intoxicated' means being under the influence of alcoholic liquor, a controlled substance, other intoxicating substance, or a combination of them; the same combined-substance language runs through the visibly-impaired prong and the special-verdict provisions. — So what: Drunk, drugged, or drunk-and-drugged driving are charged under one statute - there is no separate 'polydrug DUI' defense gap. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-257-625](https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-257-625)
- [L4] Operating with 'any amount' in the body of a controlled substance listed in Schedule 1 (MCL 333.7212) or of a substance described in MCL 333.7214(a)(iv) is a standalone misdemeanor; impairment is not an element. — So what: A driver with any detectable THC, psilocybin, or cocaine in their system can be convicted without any proof of bad driving. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-257-625](https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-257-625)
- [L4] MCL 333.7214 is MICHIGAN'S SCHEDULE 2 (not Schedule 1, and not the psilocybin cite); subsection (a)(iv) covers coca leaves and cocaine, its salts, stereoisomers and salts of stereoisomers - the OWPD statute pulls this category into zero tolerance. Psilocybin's correct cite is MCL 333.7212(1)(c), Schedule 1 hallucinogens. — So what: Driving with any amount of cocaine in the body is the same zero-tolerance misdemeanor as THC; the task brief's 'MCL 333.7214 (Schedule 1)' label for psilocybin is a miscite. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-333-7214.pdf](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-333-7214.pdf)
- [L4] First violation of MCL 257.625(1) or (8): misdemeanor, up to 93 days jail, $100-500 fine, up to 360 hours community service (high-BAC 0.17+ prong: 180 days, $200-700); second within 7 years: 5 days-1 year jail, $200-1,000; third or later: felony, 1-5 years prison, $500-5,000. — So what: Repeat impaired-driving charges escalate to felony prison exposure quickly, regardless of whether the substance was alcohol or drugs. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-257-625](https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-257-625)
- [L4] Michigan has no numeric THC blood limit; the operative standard remains any-amount presence (MCL 257.625(8)) or impairment (MCL 257.625(1)/(3)). People v Perry, 338 Mich App 363 (2021): MRTMA does not conflict with or preempt the zero-tolerance provision (under-21 context). People v Lopez-Hernandez (Mich Ct App, published July 11, 2024): MRTMA does not supersede the Vehicle Code; marijuana-abstinence probation condition enforced after marijuana-OWVI conviction - now on application at the Michigan Supreme Court (No. 167529). — So what: Buying cannabis is legal for adults; driving with any THC in your system is still a crime, and courts can also bar legal cannabis use as a probation condition. — (VERIFIED (note: Lopez-Hernandez under MSC review - flag for reversal risk)) Source: [https://www.michbar.org/Portals/0/opinions/appeals/2024/071124/81933.pdf](https://www.michbar.org/Portals/0/opinions/appeals/2024/071124/81933.pdf)
- [L4] The Michigan Medical Marihuana Act's immunity supersedes the Vehicle Code's zero-tolerance provision for a registered qualifying patient who internally possesses marijuana but is not otherwise 'under the influence' of it. — So what: A current medical card is the only driver-side shield from the any-amount THC rule - and it disappears on proof of actual impairment. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://www.courts.michigan.gov/4ab3fb/siteassets/publications/benchbooks/csbb/csbbresponsivehtml5.zip/CSBB/Ch_8_Marijuana/Operating_a_Motor_Vehicle.htm](https://www.courts.michigan.gov/4ab3fb/siteassets/publications/benchbooks/csbb/csbbresponsivehtml5.zip/CSBB/Ch_8_Marijuana/Operating_a_Motor_Vehicle.htm)
- [L4] Cocaethylene is produced in the liver only when cocaine and ethanol are co-used; it is a psychoactive metabolite with a plasma half-life roughly 3-5x cocaine's and about 30% greater toxicity than cocaine or alcohol alone, and its measurable presence indicates simultaneous use even after cocaine itself clears. — So what: One blood draw can prove both substances were on board - laboratories and prosecutors use combination toxicology to match the statutory combination theory. — (VERIFIED (medical science); the 'prosecution uses it to prove combination' line is analysis, not a cited case) Source: [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/[PMC8885871](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8885871/)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/[PMC8885871](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8885871/))
- [L4] Psilocybin and psilocyn are listed Schedule 1 hallucinogens under Michigan's Public Health Code; psilocybin is also Schedule I federally (cite flagged). — So what: Statewide, psilocybin is fully illegal in Michigan at both state and federal level, regardless of local decrim votes. — (VERIFIED (state); federal citation UNVERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-333-7212.pdf](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-333-7212.pdf)
- [L4] Possession: misdemeanor, up to 1 year and/or $2,000 (MCL 333.7403(2)(c), which names psilocyn and psilocybin). Use: misdemeanor, up to 6 months and/or $500 (MCL 333.7404(2)(c)). Manufacture, delivery, or possession with intent (the charge used for growing mushrooms): felony, up to 7 years and/or $10,000 (MCL 333.7401(2)(b)(ii), 'any other controlled substance classified in schedule 1, 2, or 3, except marihuana'). — So what: Personal possession is a misdemeanor; the moment growing or sharing enters the picture it is a 7-year felony. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-333-7401.pdf](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-333-7401.pdf)
- [L4] Ann Arbor Resolution R-20-362 (9/21/2020, unanimous); Detroit Proposal E (11/2/2021, ~61% approval, enacted as city ordinance); Hazel Park resolution (3/22/2022); Ferndale resolution (2/27/2023); Ypsilanti Resolution 2024-001 (1/9/2024, 6-0); Jackson (12/16/2025 per secondary trackers - UNVERIFIED). Washtenaw County Prosecuting Attorney non-charging policy for personal entheogen cases (announced Jan 2021). Grand Rapids adopted only a non-binding support/research resolution - NOT a lowest-enforcement-priority directive. — So what: Inside the listed cities arrest odds drop; do not count Grand Rapids, and do not count Jackson until verified. — (VERIFIED (all but Jackson, which is UNVERIFIED; Grand Rapids = support-only per multiple trackers)) Source: [https://www.mlive.com/news/ann-arbor/2024/01/these-plants-have-saved-my-life-ypsilanti-decriminalizes-psychedelic-plants-and-fungi.html](https://www.mlive.com/news/ann-arbor/2024/01/these-plants-have-saved-my-life-ypsilanti-decriminalizes-psychedelic-plants-and-fungi.html)
- [L4] The resolutions direct municipal police to make investigation/arrest for personal entheogen conduct the lowest priority and bar city funds/resources for those cases; they do not amend any MCL, do not bind the Michigan State Police, county sheriffs, county prosecutors (except Washtenaw's own policy) or federal authorities, and each resolution preserves carve-outs: minors, schools, driving under the influence, public disturbance, commercial sale/manufacture. — So what: Decriminalized here means deprioritized, not legal - state and federal law still apply everywhere in Michigan. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legistarweb-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/attachment/pdf/1792203/Mushroom_Resolution_1-18-23.pdf](https://legistarweb-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/attachment/pdf/1792203/Mushroom_Resolution_1-18-23.pdf)
- [L4] Earlier statewide decriminalization bills (SB 631 of 2021, Irwin/Hollier; SB 499 of 2023, Irwin) did not advance to enactment (final committee status UNVERIFIED). The current live bill is HB 4686 of 2025 (Rep. McFall): would add MCL 333.7404a exempting adults 18+ with a documented PTSD diagnosis who possess up to 2 ounces of psilocybin/psilocyn for personal use from MCL 333.7401/7403/7404 - introduced 6/25/2025, referred to House Families and Veterans, no hearing listed. No Oregon/Colorado-style regulated-access program exists in Michigan. — So what: No statewide psilocybin change is in force; the only pending vehicle is a narrow PTSD-medical-record exemption. — (VERIFIED (HB 4686 status); SB 631/499 outcomes UNVERIFIED; absence of regulated program is verified-by-absence in this lane) Source: [https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2025-HB-4686](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2025-HB-4686)
- [L4] For persons 21+: lawful to possess/use/internally possess/purchase/transport/process up to 2.5 oz (max 15 g as concentrate); within the residence up to 10 oz plus cultivate up to 12 plants; non-commercial gifting up to 2.5 oz to another adult. Exceeding limits slides up a civil-infraction ladder: within 2x = civil infraction (first <=$500, second <=$1,000, third+ misdemeanor <=$2,000); more than 2x = misdemeanor with no imprisonment unless habitual/willful/commercial/violent. — So what: Adult-use amounts are exact numbers, not vibes - going over converts lawful conduct into fines, then into a misdemeanor. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/chapter-333/statute-initiated-law-1-of-2018/section-333-27965/](https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/chapter-333/statute-initiated-law-1-of-2018/section-333-27965/)
- [L4] MRTMA does not authorize consuming marijuana in a public place or smoking where the property controller prohibits (MCL 333.27954(1)(e)) - except municipality-authorized designated consumption areas inaccessible to under-21s. A person within section 5 limits is civilly-infraction-track under MCL 333.27965(1) (fine <=$100; section 4(1)(e) is not among its carve-outs to criminal statutes - reading corroborated by the MALPH penalty chart). By contrast, consuming while operating any vehicle or smoking in the passenger area (MCL 333.27954(1)(g)) is carved OUT to criminal treatment (MCL 333.7404(2)(d), 90-day misdemeanor, per MALPH chart). — So what: Street/park/bar consumption is a civil fine; lighting up behind the wheel is a crime on top of the OWI/OWPD exposure. — (VERIFIED (statutes); the 4(1)(e)-to-27965(1) penalty mapping is a structural reading corroborated by secondary chart - flag) Source: [https://www.malph.org/sites/default/files/MRTMA%20Penalty%20Chart%20%2004082019.pdf](https://www.malph.org/sites/default/files/MRTMA%20Penalty%20Chart%20%2004082019.pdf)
- [L4] A person shall not use, possess, sell, or offer for sale marijuana-infused beer, wine, mixed wine drink, mixed spirit drink, or spirits - misdemeanor (added by 2018 PA 346, HB 4668). Liquor licensees may not allow the sale, possession, or consumption on the licensed premises of any controlled substance prohibited by the Public Health Code (MLCC Rule 436.1011(6)(d)). CRA-designated consumption establishments operate under Marihuana Operations Rule R 420.203(2) (food only with other authorizations; an express alcohol-service ban was not located - UNVERIFIED). — So what: No THC-beer or weed-wine sales in Michigan; bars cannot allow cannabis, and cannabis lounges cannot pour alcohol. — (VERIFIED (436.1914b + 436.1011); CRA express alcohol ban UNVERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-436-1914b](https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-436-1914b)
- [L4] MRTMA does not require an employer to permit or accommodate marijuana conduct in the workplace or on employer property, does not bar discipline for workplace drug-policy violations or for working under the influence, and allows refusal to hire, discharge, or other adverse action on those grounds. — So what: A legal purchase does not equal a protected habit - zero-tolerance workplace drug policies survive legalization. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-333-27954](https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-333-27954)
- [L4] MMMA qualifying conditions (MCL 333.26423(b)): cancer, glaucoma, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis C, ALS, Crohn's, agitation of Alzheimer's, nail patella, plus treatment-produced cachexia/severe chronic pain/severe nausea/seizures/severe persistent muscle spasms, plus agency-approved additions. LARA approved 11 more in 2018 (arthritis, autism, chronic pain, colitis, IBD, OCD, Parkinson's, rheumatoid arthritis, spinal cord injury, Tourette's, ulcerative colitis) and DENIED anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, asthma, brain injury, diabetes, panic attacks, and others. PTSD is on the qualifying list. No alcohol-related condition (alcohol use disorder, alcohol-associated anxiety/depression) appears on any qualifying list. — So what: The medical pathway is condition-based: PTSD can qualify a person; alcohol-linked diagnoses explicitly do not. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://michigan.gov/cra/spotlight/lara-director-approves-eleven-new-debilitating-medical-conditions-for-michigan-medical-marihuana-pa](https://michigan.gov/cra/spotlight/lara-director-approves-eleven-new-debilitating-medical-conditions-for-michigan-medical-marihuana-pa)
- [L4] A person may apply to set aside all Michigan convictions if they have no more than 3 felony convictions total (max 2 assaultive crimes set aside lifetime; max 1 felony for the same offense punishable by more than 10 years). Waiting periods run from the last of sentence imposition, probation completion, parole discharge, or imprisonment completion: 3 years for non-serious misdemeanors, 5 years for one felony/serious misdemeanors/first-violation OWI, 7 years for more than one felony; $50 state police fee; no pending charges and no new convictions during the period; setting aside is discretionary, 'a privilege and conditional and is not a right.' — So what: Old drug convictions are clearable on this clock - a psilocybin possession misdemeanor after 3 years, a cocaine possession felony after 5. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-780-621](https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-780-621)
- [L4] OWI convictions are barred from set-aside EXCEPT a 'first violation operating while intoxicated offense' - defined by MCL 780.621(4)(d) to include MCL 257.625(1) (OWI incl. drugs/high-BAC), (2), (3), (6), (8) (any Schedule 1/cocaine presence) and equivalents - which may be set aside once in a lifetime, 5+ years after the last of sentence/probation/parole/imprisonment, by petition (form MC 228) with prosecutor/AG objection rights; the court may weigh rehabilitative or educational programming; first-violation OWI is expressly excluded from automatic set-aside (MCL 780.621c(3)); and a set-aside does NOT remove the conviction from the Secretary of State driving record (MCL 780.621c(5)). Excluded: OWI causing death/serious injury, child endangerment, commercial-vehicle offenses, repeat OWI. — So what: One clean-slate shot exists for a first OWI - including drug OWPD convictions - but the license record stays dirty regardless. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-780-621C](https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-780-621C)
- [L4] Automatic (no application) set-asides began Apr 11, 2023: misdemeanors punishable by <=92 days after 7 years from sentence; felonies after 10 years from last of sentence/completion of imprisonment; lifetime caps of 2 felonies + 4 misdemeanors (caps do not apply to the <=92-day class); excluded classes include assaultive crimes, serious misdemeanors, crimes of dishonesty, offenses punishable by 10+ years, crimes against minors/vulnerable adults, human trafficking. Separately, MCL 780.621e (since Jan 1, 2020): a person convicted of misdemeanor marijuana offenses (possession MCL 333.7403(2)(d), use MCL 333.7404(2)(d), paraphernalia MCL 333.7453) gets a rebuttable presumption the conduct is no longer criminal if committed after Dec 6, 2018 - prosecutor bears the rebuttal burden. Michigan Legal Help reports MSP estimated ~1,000,000 convictions set aside on day one. — So what: Old low-level marijuana convictions largely clear themselves; the 90-day marijuana-use misdemeanor auto-expires after 7 years. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-780-621G](https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-780-621G)
- [L4] Michigan Legal Help maintains a 'Clearing a Criminal Record' hub (expungement of adult convictions, juvenile adjudications, fixing record mistakes, license restoration), a free Do-It-Yourself Expungement (Adult Conviction) form tool via LawHelp Interactive, an 'Automatic Expungement' explainer, and a Guide to Legal Help referral tool; expungement fairs with volunteer lawyers occur around the state; the court form is MC 228 with a $50 MSP fee. — So what: The DIY expungement route is free and real - start there, and use the Guide to Legal Help to find legal aid for complicated records. — (VERIFIED) Source: [https://michiganlegalhelp.org/resources/clearing-criminal-record](https://michiganlegalhelp.org/resources/clearing-criminal-record)

⚠ This lane is educational information for a community harm-reduction study guide - it is not legal advice and creates no attorney-client relationship; statutes and cases change, so verify current text (legislature.mi.gov) and consult a licensed Michigan attorney or Michigan Legal Help for any specific case.

concepts.title: Ch. 7 — The tincture question: the evidence-based verdict is NO
concepts.text:
The community asked a chemist's question: could a half-pint of 80-proof spirits holding a few grams of dried mushroom material and a fraction of a gram of cocaine work as a sublingual “microdose tincture” for functional use? The proposal is named here only as the object of analysis — this guide does not provide, endorse, or optimize any preparation.

THE VERDICT — NO. By pharmacology this is not a microdose tincture. It is a three-drug concentrate whose dose cannot be known pour to pour, whose active molecules disagree with their own solvent, and which sits inside the two most dangerous documented pairing classes in this corpus (alcohol × cocaine = cocaethylene; stimulant × serotonergic = two pressor systems stacking). You cannot calibrate what you cannot extract uniformly — and the stated goal, sub-perceptual functional dosing, is the first thing the chemistry defeats.

Evidence-based anchors (published, sourced):
- Solvent mismatch: psilocybin is a water-soluble zwitterionic phosphate ester, so ethanol is a poor solvent for it — alkaloids come out partial and non-uniform, and no quantitative ethanol-versus-water efficiency study exists (UNVERIFIED, lane 2).
- The cocaine column is never “micro”: a 30 mL pour of the proposed mixture carries roughly 15–30 mg of cocaine — up to half of a published 50–100 mg line — before any question of how much actually dissolved.
- Potency variance: published LC-MS/MS surveys put psilocybin at 0.14–0.42% and psilocin at 0.37–1.30% of dry weight, so a bottle of that scale holds on the order of 10–50 mg of total tryptamine alkaloids — between 0.4× and 2× a full 25 mg clinical dose — before unknown losses nobody can measure at home.
- Ethanol load: a half-pint of 80-proof holds about 63 g of ethanol ≈ 4.5 standard drinks in the bottle itself — and ethanol is the in-body reactant for cocaethylene (≈17% ± 6% conversion) and a stop-signal masker on top.
- Sublingual promise is shaky: clinical psilocybin is dosed orally, no dedicated human sublingual PK study exists, and swallowed fraction behaves like an edible.

Legal reality (Michigan): one container like this is manufacture-scale exposure — psilocybin manufacture or delivery is a 7-year felony (MCL 333.7401(2)(b)(ii)), cocaine is Schedule 2 (MCL 333.7214(a)(iv)), and any amount of either in the body plus driving is the zero-tolerance offense (MCL 257.625(8)).

concepts.title: Ch. 7 — Boundary receipt: the refusal, stated plainly
concepts.text:
This guide does not provide a preparation protocol, optimization advice, or dose-standardization methods for Schedule 1 or Schedule 2 substances — not for this question, not for any question, however reasonable the ask sounds.

That refusal is not a judgment of the people asking. It is the line that keeps the guide legal, publishable, and honest: the moment a health-education document starts teaching preparation, it stops being health education.

What this guide does instead:
- Answers the safety question with evidence, labeled shelf by shelf.
- Names the real risk drivers: non-uniform pours, masked stop-signals, the liver's third-drug factory, and felony-grade legal exposure in one container.
- Points at the pattern with literature behind it — single-substance windows, cardiac and mental-health screening, journaling, peer support.

⚠ If someone is already doing this: expect non-uniform doses (the same pour is not the same dose twice), do not add more alcohol to the window, run the three screening questions (psychosis or bipolar history? lithium or MAOI? is the schedule driven by need rather than protocol?), keep a sober sitter, treat chest pain or loss of consciousness as a 911 call, and know the Clean Slate doorway if a record gets created.

concepts.title: Action pathways — information, not representation
concepts.text:
The legal chapter of this corpus is information, not representation. Nothing here is legal advice, nothing here creates an attorney-client relationship, and statutes and cases change — verify current text on legislature.mi.gov and consult a licensed Michigan attorney or Michigan Legal Help for any specific case.

What Michigan actually offers, as the lane read it from primary sources:
- Clean Slate, MCL 780.621 et seq.: old drug convictions clear on a clock — a psilocybin possession misdemeanor after 3 years, a cocaine possession felony after 5, with caps and waiting periods set by MCL 780.621d.
- One clean-slate shot for a first-offense OWI, including drug-driving OWPD (MCL 780.621c(1)(d)(i), (3)–(5); 780.621d(2); 780.621(4)(d)) — though the license record stays dirty regardless.
- Automatic set-asides (MCL 780.621g, 780.621e): old low-level marijuana convictions largely clear themselves — a 90-day marijuana-use misdemeanor auto-expires after 7 years.
- The free DIY route: Michigan Legal Help’s “Clearing a Criminal Record” plus state form MC 228, with the Guide to Legal Help for complicated records.

⚠ Not legal advice — and not a promise about anyone’s case: eligibility depends on the record itself. For a medical emergency (chest pain, loss of consciousness, suspected overdose) the number is 911, not a study guide.

concepts.title: Sources & provenance — how to re-check anything here
concepts.text:
Corpus: Sarah's alcohol × substances research transfer, delivered to this guide 2026-10-17 — 98 sourced findings across 6 lanes, from research lanes deleg_42d12d7c (lanes 1–4) and deleg_d75204e2 (lanes 5–6). The Ch. 7 chapter file arrived the same day and is summarized here as Ch. 7.

Every finding below carries exactly the source its lane recorded: PMC and PubMed identifiers and DOIs resolve to working links, Michigan statutes resolve to legislature.mi.gov, and citation-only sources (books, technical bulletins, organization guidance) print verbatim as recorded rather than being linked to a guessed URL.

Stamp: sources read 2026-10-17. Fast-moving legal claims — city resolutions, bill status — can move under an old stamp; re-check legislature.mi.gov before relying on any legal figure.

Sibling corpus for cross-reference: the harm-reduction kit playbook and substance-testing tiers (2026-10-03) are summarized in the Michigan Drug Policy & Harm Reduction module — naloxone access, fentanyl test strips and the four testing tiers live there, not here.

Re-check habit: pick any claim, follow its link, and confirm it says what this guide says it says. A dead link or a moved claim means the claim needs re-verifying.

examples.title: “Cocaethylene is just the nicer high — it isn't dangerous”
examples.scenario: Someone at the table waves off the alcohol-plus-cocaine warning as scare tactics from people who have never tried it.
examples.outcome: Cocaethylene is made in the liver by hCE1/hCE2 transesterification, has roughly cocaine's dopamine-reuptake potency, clears about 20% slower, and carries an 18–25× sudden-death association in a 2024 systematic review — about 21.5× with coronary disease, with cocaethylene present in ~76% of cocaine-related sudden deaths in one cohort. In one ED cohort cardiac arrest ran 6.1% with cocaethylene versus 0.67% with cocaine alone. The discomfort people feel about this pairing is documented; the confidence that it is fine is not.

examples.title: “It's decrim in my city, so it's legal”
examples.scenario: A friend plans a trip carrying psilocybin openly because their city passed a lowest-enforcement-priority resolution.
examples.outcome: Decrim means deprioritized, not legal. State (MCL 333.7212(1)(c)) and federal Schedule I law still apply everywhere in Michigan, local arrest odds only drop, and selling or distributing was never touched. The corpus flags the Jackson resolution as UNVERIFIED (secondary trackers only) and Grand Rapids as support-only with conflicting details — two more reasons not to build a plan on a city map.

examples.title: “I drink first, so I'll know my limit when I smoke”
examples.scenario: Someone drinks a few, then uses cannabis, expecting the alcohol signal to stay honest.
examples.outcome: It runs the other way: controlled trials show alcohol before cannabis raises peak blood THC and speeds onset (Lukas 2001; Hartman 2015, n=19), while cannabis dulls perceived alcohol effects so people keep drinking — and cannabis's antiemetic effect can suppress vomiting, one of the body's warnings for alcohol toxicity. Blackouts are the signature harm: ~56% of simultaneous users versus ~37% and ~28% in the comparison groups.

pitfalls: MYTH: “Each substance alone is fine, so the mix is fine.” Documented pairing harms are additive — blackouts, at-least-additive driving impairment, and alcohol as the top companion in cocaine ED visits.

MYTH: “A psychedelic makes me feel less drunk, so I am less drunk.” Barrett 2000 found the felt alcohol effect dimmed in about 60% of psilocybin co-users (86.7% with LSD) while blood alcohol itself is unchanged.
A medical cannabis card does not protect a driver: People v Koon makes a current card the only driver-side shield from the any-amount THC rule, and it disappears on proof of actual impairment.
MCL 257.625(8) needs no bad driving — any detectable amount of a controlled substance plus driving is the offense. “I wasn't impaired” is not a defense to it.
Corrected citations matter: cocaine is MCL 333.7214(a)(iv) (Schedule 2), psilocybin is MCL 333.7212(1)(c). Repeating a miscite from an old brief is how a study guide misleads a real case.
